frictionVectors.title: EU Energy Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian gas while pressing Algiers on migration, market access, and political issues. Sonatrach retains strong control over upstream assets and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Algeria's support for Polisario sustains strategic tension with Morocco, complicating regional trade, security coordination, and trans-Maghreb infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese finance and construction remain important to Angola's transport and energy infrastructure, although Luanda is seeking greater creditor diversification and fiscal autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues still dominate external earnings, leaving sovereign resource control vulnerable to production declines, price volatility, and foreign-operator technology dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Insecurity Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist activity near the Burkina Faso and Niger borders threatens roads, agricultural zones, and state access to northern resources. Benin is strengthening regional security partnerships while trying to avoid overdependence on any external guarantor.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's role as a regional gateway creates leverage but also exposes Benin to shifting trade relations with Nigeria, Niger, and foreign logistics operators.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has secured significant value and domestic beneficiation from diamonds, but its fiscal position remains exposed to De Beers' marketing reach and global diamond demand.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Capacity Gap
frictionVectors.details: Interest in copper, rare earths, and other minerals is growing, yet Botswana still needs foreign capital, technology, and infrastructure to convert geological potential into sovereign industrial control.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is pressing for greater state participation and local processing in gold mining, challenging established foreign operators and increasing legal and investor friction.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Alignment
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou's reliance on Russian security support reduces Western influence but introduces new dependency risks, while insecurity continues to disrupt mining corridors and state revenue collection.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda–Burundi security rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and cross-border destabilization keep the frontier tense, while Burundi’s role in eastern DRC complicates regional diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance gap
frictionVectors.details: Gold, nickel and rare-earth prospects attract foreign interest, but weak oversight and limited infrastructure constrain the state’s ability to capture value.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime-security competition
frictionVectors.details: Mindelo and other maritime assets draw interest from European, North American and Chinese-linked actors, creating pressure to preserve strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and tourism dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains exposed to external tourism, remittances and development finance, limiting resilience despite strong institutions and stable governance.

frictionVectors.title: Oil, gas and mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital remains central to hydrocarbons, mining and major infrastructure, while opaque contracting and limited local processing reduce sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict across border regions
frictionVectors.details: The Anglophone conflict, Boko Haram-linked violence in the Far North and instability near the Central African Republic disrupt transport and weaken effective state control.

frictionVectors.title: Russian-linked mining and security influence
frictionVectors.details: Russian security contractors and associated commercial networks retain major influence around regime protection and mineral access, limiting transparency and bargaining autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-group control of resource zones
frictionVectors.details: Gold and diamond production in insecure areas remains vulnerable to informal taxation and smuggling, while roads and border corridors are highly unreliable.

frictionVectors.title: External security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The government is balancing relationships with France, Russia-linked actors, Gulf states and neighboring regimes as it seeks security support without surrendering strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Oil infrastructure and border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on oil exports and vulnerable pipeline routes leaves public finances exposed, while Sudan’s war and armed activity around Lake Chad increase logistical and humanitarian pressure.

highlights: Indian Ocean leverage, limited bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: French control over Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, making the territorial dispute a persistent sovereignty issue for Moroni. The dispute also shapes maritime access, migration policy, and external security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on external financing and partners for ports, energy, and transport infrastructure. Gulf, French, and other foreign interests compete for influence without giving Comoros substantial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper dependency
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms dominate much of the formal mining value chain, while the state struggles to secure taxation, processing capacity, and environmental compliance. Chinese-linked investment remains especially influential in battery minerals.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and regional intervention
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east continues to undermine Kinshasa's territorial authority and mineral governance. Rwanda-linked security concerns, regional diplomacy, and competing external interests constrain the government's freedom of action.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: Public finances and export earnings remain heavily tied to oil, leaving the state exposed to price cycles and foreign technical and commercial partners. Limited domestic refining and diversification reduce sovereign control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction are central to roads, public works, and resource-linked infrastructure. Debt obligations and opaque contracting can narrow policy flexibility even where projects improve connectivity.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa and commodity dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire has expanded domestic processing and regulatory capacity, but foreign buyers and volatile global prices still capture significant value. Sustainability rules and financing conditions imposed abroad create additional pressure on producers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and security competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port and logistics expansion increases national leverage, while Gulf, European, and Asian investors compete for infrastructure access. Sahel instability also raises the cost of protecting transport corridors and northern supply routes.

frictionVectors.title: Base-economy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position through foreign military facilities, but security rents make the economy dependent on external powers. The United States, China, France, Japan, and others create revenue while competing for strategic influence.

frictionVectors.title: Port debt and Ethiopian reliance
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's ports remain vital to Ethiopia's trade, yet large infrastructure debts and foreign operating interests limit the state's room for maneuver. Any disruption in Ethiopian demand or regional security would expose major fiscal and strategic vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and strategic asset dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy external financing needs increase reliance on Gulf investors, multilateral lenders, and asset monetization. This can constrain policy autonomy around ports, logistics, and major infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains the central sovereignty and resource-security concern. Egypt continues to seek binding operating guarantees while balancing diplomacy with deterrence.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature fields and limited economic diversification weaken sovereign fiscal control. Foreign technical expertise and investment remain important to sustaining offshore production.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, ports, and public works provide critical connectivity but increase exposure to creditor and contractor influence. Utilization and repayment risks remain significant.

frictionVectors.title: Regional military entanglement
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's strategic coastline and proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb expose it to competition among Red Sea states and external powers. Tensions with Ethiopia and broader regional conflicts could disrupt sovereignty calculations.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led mining provides scarce export revenue but leaves the state dependent on a narrow resource base and external operators. Sanctions risk and limited investment access constrain bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Economic dependence on South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Trade, remittances, food supply, and transport links are heavily tied to South Africa and the Southern African Customs Union. This limits Eswatini's room to pursue fully autonomous economic and foreign policies.

frictionVectors.title: Investment and governance risk
frictionVectors.details: Political unrest and governance concerns can deter diversified investment beyond sugar, textiles, and agro-processing. External partners retain leverage through market access and development finance.

frictionVectors.title: Debt restructuring and foreign finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressure and reliance on multilateral and bilateral creditors constrain Addis Ababa's control over infrastructure and macroeconomic policy. Restructuring efforts are intended to restore autonomy but require difficult reforms.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and port competition
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Egypt and efforts to secure reliable Red Sea access place water, ports, and regional corridors at the center of national strategy. These initiatives risk sharper confrontation with neighbors and external stakeholders.

highlights: Manganese and oil remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: Mining Dependence and Contract Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked operators remain central to manganese production and infrastructure, limiting Libreville's bargaining power despite efforts to increase domestic processing and state participation.

frictionVectors.title: French Influence Recalibration
frictionVectors.details: Gabon is diversifying diplomatic and security ties after the end of Bongo-era alignment, but French commercial and security networks remain influential.

highlights: Senegal remains the essential external partner

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese Economic and Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for trade routes, energy connectivity, and regional security, creating resilience but constraining independent policy choices.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and Maritime Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fishing and weak monitoring continue to threaten coastal livelihoods and state revenue, reinforcing concerns over unequal access to marine resources.

highlights: Gold remains the core sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Gold Mining
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey damages waterways, agricultural land, and public institutions while enabling foreign-linked trading networks to capture value outside formal state channels.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Resource-Finance Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF conditions constrain spending and policy autonomy, while offshore oil and mineral revenues remain vulnerable to external financing and commodity cycles.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Strategic Corridor
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project ties Guinea to Chinese, Singaporean, and Western investors while rail and port infrastructure create long-term leverage over national export sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Bargaining Imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Guinea remains a leading bauxite exporter but captures limited downstream value, with foreign firms retaining substantial influence over logistics, refining, and marketing.

highlights: Cashew exports sustain a fragile political economy
Security institutions remain vulnerable to elite capture

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Value-Chain Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends heavily on raw cashew exports, leaving producers exposed to foreign buyers, price volatility, and limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Illicit-Trade Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Weak maritime enforcement and politicized security structures leave ports and coastal routes vulnerable to narcotics trafficking and external commercial influence.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressures are constraining fiscal autonomy and complicating negotiations with multilateral lenders and bilateral creditors. Strategic transport and energy infrastructure remains tied to foreign financing and contractors.

frictionVectors.title: Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is deepening security cooperation with the United States and other partners, particularly against al-Shabaab, while seeking to preserve decision-making autonomy and regional influence.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but leave Lesotho dependent on a single dominant market and vulnerable to disputes over pricing, delays, and project control.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Textile Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower and garment production remain exposed to external capital, imported inputs, and changing trade preferences. Limited diversification weakens domestic leverage over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and other resource projects attract foreign capital and infrastructure commitments, but concession terms, local value addition, and revenue capture remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Logistics Influence
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia-linked logistics and major industrial projects are heavily reliant on external operators and financiers. This creates infrastructure benefits while limiting Liberia's control over trade bottlenecks.

highlights: Foreign Powers at the Infrastructure Gate

frictionVectors.title: Oil Production Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed networks continue to use oil fields, export terminals, and budget access as leverage. The divided security environment prevents consistent national control of the energy sector.

frictionVectors.title: External Military and Energy Influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign states and private security actors retain influence through military support, reconstruction interests, and energy partnerships. Their involvement reinforces fragmentation and complicates unified infrastructure planning.

frictionVectors.title: Large-Scale Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, and mineral-sands projects bring export earnings and infrastructure but leave Madagascar exposed to foreign operators, commodity cycles, and disputes over taxation and environmental costs.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Infrastructure Financing
frictionVectors.details: External lenders and investors influence ports, energy, and transport development, while weak domestic capacity limits the state's ability to capture full strategic value from these assets.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCE LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-backed reforms constrain policy space, while foreign creditors and donors retain significant influence over public investment and essential imports.

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND MINING BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Persistent electricity shortages and reliance on imported fuel undermine industrial sovereignty, while emerging mining projects raise concerns over contract transparency and domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY FOOTPRINT
frictionVectors.details: The transition from Wagner-linked forces toward Russian Africa Corps support deepens military dependence on Moscow while providing limited durable improvement in territorial security.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD GOVERNANCE AND SANCTIONS
frictionVectors.details: State efforts to raise its share of gold revenues face investor and operator resistance, while regional sanctions, insecurity, and opaque contracting constrain sovereign control over the mining sector.

highlights: Balancing China, Europe, and Gulf Capital

frictionVectors.title: GTA GAS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project expands export revenues but leaves Mauritania reliant on foreign operators, offshore infrastructure, and Senegal-linked arrangements for production and monetization.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND INFRASTRUCTURE CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore remains central to the economy, with Chinese and other foreign capital prominent in logistics and mining; weak local processing limits domestic value capture.

highlights: Strategic Autonomy in the Indian Ocean

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS AND MARITIME SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over the Chagos Archipelago and continued foreign military access remain sensitive tests of Mauritius's sovereignty, despite improved diplomatic leverage over the issue.

frictionVectors.title: IMPORT-DEPENDENT ENERGY SYSTEM
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutional control but remains exposed to imported fuel costs, external shipping disruptions, and foreign investment conditions in port and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE DIPLOMACY
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses phosphate, fisheries, renewable-energy, and port development to consolidate control in Western Sahara, generating continuing legal and diplomatic friction with Algeria, the Polisario Front, and some foreign partners.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN CAPITAL AND WATER PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and U.S. investment accelerates ports, renewables, and manufacturing, but drought and water scarcity could limit the sovereign benefits of industrial expansion.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of LNG value chain
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies and lenders retain decisive influence over project financing, contracting, and export revenues. Maputo is seeking stronger domestic participation without jeopardizing the delayed LNG revival.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent attacks continue to threaten gas infrastructure and local legitimacy. Rwanda and other external security partners provide essential support, increasing Maputo's dependence on outside forces.

highlights: Offshore oil stakes reshape sovereignty debate

frictionVectors.title: Foreign participation in offshore hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: New oil discoveries could expand fiscal space but leave Namibia dependent on foreign capital, technology, and operators. The government is under pressure to secure stronger local-content and revenue terms.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals infrastructure gap
frictionVectors.details: Lithium, uranium, and green-hydrogen projects attract Gulf, European, and Asian partners. Limited domestic processing and transport capacity risks locking Namibia into an exporter role.

highlights: Western security ties give way to Sahel bloc

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and mining renegotiations
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is pressing foreign operators for greater state control and fiscal returns, especially in uranium. Contract disputes and declining external confidence threaten investment and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: The oil-export corridor and major transport routes remain vulnerable to insurgency, sabotage, and regional political disruption. Reliance on military partners outside the former Western security architecture creates new dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital and oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria is strengthening local participation and attracting new investment, but production, refining, and offshore development still depend heavily on foreign finance and technology. Divestments and regulatory uncertainty complicate state control.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and pipeline insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Power shortages, gas-supply bottlenecks, theft, and attacks on pipelines limit the conversion of resource wealth into sovereign industrial capacity. Private infrastructure projects are expanding but remain exposed to security and regulatory risks.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo mineral supply chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security and commercial networks in eastern DRC face sustained international scrutiny over alleged support to M23 and mineral flows. Sanctions pressure and diplomatic isolation could constrain access to technology, finance, and markets.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and investment dependence
frictionVectors.details: Kigali retains strong state capacity but relies on external donors, lenders, and investors for infrastructure and development finance. Conditionality over regional security and political governance limits complete strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea oil blocks
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe is seeking exploration investment while avoiding overreliance on external operators. Limited discoveries and weak fiscal capacity constrain immediate sovereign leverage.

frictionVectors.title: External maritime security
frictionVectors.details: European and regional partners provide maritime-security support, creating useful capacity but leaving the archipelago dependent on outside surveillance and enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The new government is pressing for greater national value from offshore production and a review of prior agreements. Delays, investor uncertainty, and revenue-management challenges could weaken near-term control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fleets, including foreign vessels operating through licensing arrangements, continue to strain fisheries and coastal livelihoods. Enforcement capacity and transparency remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles is strengthening sustainable fisheries management and surveillance, but its economy remains exposed to powerful distant-water fleets and external market demand.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean security competition
frictionVectors.details: Port calls, maritime surveillance cooperation, and infrastructure engagement by India, France, China, and other partners provide benefits while complicating strategic neutrality.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains vital to exports but leaves the state exposed to foreign operators, commodity cycles, and disputes over taxation, local benefits, and environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese-backed infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign financing supports roads, energy, and mining logistics, yet repayment obligations and project-linked resource access can narrow policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and offshore concessions
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and other external actors compete for port, logistics, and prospective offshore-resource access. Federal-regional disputes make concession legitimacy and revenue sharing especially sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: External security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Somalia relies heavily on foreign military, financial, and training support against al-Shabaab and maritime insecurity. This assistance is essential but limits independent control over security priorities and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY AND GRID DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability is improving unevenly, but Eskom’s financial and maintenance constraints continue to limit industrial sovereignty. Private generation and foreign capital are filling gaps while increasing regulatory and ownership sensitivities.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL CONGESTION
frictionVectors.details: Chronic rail and port failures constrain coal, iron-ore, and mineral exports. Reform partnerships involving private and international operators may improve throughput but could dilute public control over strategic logistics.

frictionVectors.title: SUDAN PIPELINE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan’s oil exports depend on infrastructure crossing war-affected Sudan, leaving production, revenue, and market access exposed to external coercion and repeated disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE REVENUE CAPTURE
frictionVectors.details: Oil income remains central to state financing but is weakened by opaque contracts, arrears, elite patronage, and insecurity. Foreign operators retain significant leverage over production and export logistics.

highlights: Gold and ports drive external competition

frictionVectors.title: GOLD NETWORKS AND WAR FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling remain major sources of leverage for armed actors and their external partners. Weak oversight allows foreign traders and security-linked networks to capture value outside formal state channels.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA PORT COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan is a strategic lifeline and a focus of competing Gulf, Russian, and regional interests. Wartime dependence on external shipping, finance, and security support limits Khartoum’s effective control over maritime infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: LNG PROJECT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over large offshore gas development continue to balance state revenue, local content, environmental concerns, and international investor demands. Delays preserve bargaining room but postpone broader domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND CORRIDOR CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is tightening local-processing and revenue rules for minerals while expanding rail and port links. Chinese, Gulf, and Western interests compete for access to infrastructure and critical-mineral supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE AND CONCESSIONS
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé provides major regional leverage but relies on foreign shipping, logistics, and infrastructure capital. Concession structures and opaque procurement create continuing concerns over long-term strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Instability near the northern border pressures transport corridors and security budgets. Togo must balance regional military cooperation and external security assistance against its autonomy and commercial access priorities.

frictionVectors.title: European migration leverage
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains dependent on European financial and trade relationships, while migration-control agreements expose sovereignty to external conditionality.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: High dependence on imported hydrocarbons and limited investment in domestic renewables constrain strategic autonomy and increase exposure to foreign suppliers.

frictionVectors.title: Lake Albert oil dependency
frictionVectors.details: The Tilenga and Kingfisher projects promise major revenues but rely heavily on foreign capital, technology, and export infrastructure, concentrating environmental and sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: East African pipeline exposure
frictionVectors.details: The proposed crude export route through Tanzania deepens reliance on cross-border infrastructure and external project finance while remaining vulnerable to regulatory, activist, and geopolitical pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: Copper remains the fiscal backbone, but smelting, processing, trading, and new mining investment are strongly shaped by foreign firms, limiting domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Power shortages constrain mining
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower weakness and drought-driven electricity deficits threaten mineral output, increasing dependence on regional power imports and private infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lithium, platinum, gold, and other mineral projects attract Chinese and other foreign capital, but weak transparency and limited local processing constrain sovereign gains.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and sanctions exposure
frictionVectors.details: Persistent monetary instability, restricted access to international finance, and Western sanctions increase reliance on informal markets and politically aligned external partners.
